name: Abiud
title: Descendant of Zerubbabel in Jesus' messianic lineage
summary: Abiud is listed in the genealogy of the Gospel of Matthew as the son of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim, forming a crucial link in the messianic lineage from King David to Joseph, Jesus' earthly father. It is notable that he is not mentioned among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chronicles 3:19–20, likely due to differing family traditions or because the term "son" was used in an extended sense in Semitic culture. Abiud probably lived during the early Persian period following the return from the Babylonian exile—a time marked by the rebuilding of the temple and renewed hope for the fulfillment of God's covenant promises. Although nothing is known about his personal life beyond the genealogy, his place in the lineage carries theological significance: he represents a link in the fulfillment of God's promise to David of an eternal throne, a promise that, according to Christian understanding, found its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Abiud's presence in the lineage testifies to God's faithfulness across generations, even during a period when David's line no longer sat on the throne.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Jesus' genealogy
keyEvents.description: Abiud is listed as the son of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim in Matthew's genealogy from Abraham to Jesus Christ.

keyEvents.title: Link in the Davidic line
keyEvents.description: Abiud connects the royal line from David through the exile period into the post-exilic era, as part of God's plan of salvation. Matthew structures the genealogy into three groups of fourteen generations to emphasize the divine order in salvation history.

keyEvents.title: Historical Context: Zerubbabel and the Rebuilding
keyEvents.description: Zerubbabel, Abiud's father according to Matthew's genealogy, led Jews back from the Babylonian exile and was central to rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. Abiud is not mentioned among Zerubbabel's sons in Chronicles, which may be due to different genealogical traditions or the use of 'son' in an extended sense.

keyEvents.title: The Messianic Promise Continued
keyEvents.description: Through Abiud, God's promise to David of an eternal throne was passed down through generations—a promise that, according to Christian belief, was fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

versions.title: Descendant of David in Jesus' Lineage
versions.reason: [minor] The title is clear, but could be refined slightly to highlight his specific position in the lineage.; [major] The role 'patriarch' is misleading. In the biblical sense, the patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Abiud is a person in the genealogy with no known leadership role. A more appropriate title would be 'ancestor of Jesus' or 'forefather'.; [minor] The reference to Eliakim is correct according to Matt 1:13. The ID format 'eljakim' looks fine, but note that there are several Eliakims in the Bible – here it refers to the Eliakim in Jesus' lineage.; [minor] Including the entire Matt 1:1-16 as a scripture reference for one link in the genealogy is unnecessarily broad. It would be more precise to limit this to verse 13 and possibly verses 1 and 17 as framing verses.; [major] The title 'Sons of Zerubbabel' is misleading – the event concerns Zerubbabel's role, not his sons. Furthermore: 1 Chron 3:19 lists Zerubbabel's sons, but Abiud is NOT mentioned among them. Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chron 3:19-20 are Meshullam and Hananiah (plus others). Abiud appears only in Matthew's genealogy. This is a well-known discrepancy that should be noted as a footnote, and the event should be rephrased.; [major] Ezra 3:2,8 (bookId 15) concerns Zerubbabel building the temple, not his sons. The title and content do not match the scripture references. The reference to 1 Chron 3:19 is relevant for Zerubbabel's children, but as noted, Abiud is missing from that list.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding the well-known discrepancy between Matthew's genealogy (which mentions Abiud as a son of Zerubbabel) and 1 Chronicles 3:19-20 (which does not mention Abiud among Zerubbabel's sons), as well as a linguistic note about the name Abiud.

footnotes.text: The name Abiud (Greek: Ἀβιούδ) may be derived from Hebrew אֲבִיהוּד (Avihud), meaning 'my father is majesty' or 'father of honor.' The name appears only in the genealogy of the Gospel of Matthew and is not found in the Old Testament.

A well-known challenge is that Abiud is not listed among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chronicles 3:19–20, where the sons Meshullam and Hananiah are named. Several explanations have been proposed: Abiud may have been an alternative name for one of the mentioned sons, he could have been a grandson counted as a 'son' in Semitic genealogy, or Matthew may have followed a different family tradition than Chronicles.

Zerubbabel led the first group of Jews back from the Babylonian exile around 538 BC and was central to rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem (completed around 516 BC). Abiud would thus have lived in the early Persian period, a time marked by reconstruction and religious renewal.

In rabbinic tradition and Jewish genealogical practice, the term 'son of' (ben) could be used more broadly to include grandchildren or later descendants. This may explain differences between various biblical genealogies.

Matthew's genealogy follows the royal line through Solomon, while Luke's genealogy follows a different line through Nathan, another son of David. Abiud appears only in Matthew's version, highlighting that the two evangelists use different genealogical traditions to emphasize distinct theological points.

During the Persian period (ca. 539–332 BC), Judah had the status of a province (Yehud Medinata) under Persian rule. Descendants of the Davidic royal family retained some social standing, even though they no longer held political power. Abiud's placement in this period reflects the transition from a royal dynasty to a more symbolic role for David's lineage.
